subtype: Approach: a shared expense sheet and advance deposit [Action]
passage:
Saturday. Tushar opened a shared sheet with columns for date, item, who paid and amount. Six friends each sent a first deposit into one account, and Harish took charge of checking that all six had arrived.

Tuesday, on the road. Every ticket, tea stop and cab fare went into the sheet within the hour. When the guesthouse was paid from the pooled money, Harish pinned the receipt photo beside that row.

The Monday after. The sheet showed a small balance left over. Nobody asked who owed what. Tushar split the remainder six ways and sent each share back. Harish said quietly that the sheet had settled the argument before it could start. Two friends who had quarrelled over a trip last year just laughed and closed the laptop.

qa.q: How many friends sent a first deposit into the one account?
qa.a: Six friends each sent a first deposit into one account.

qa.q: Why did Harish say quietly that the sheet had settled the argument before it started?
qa.a: Harish felt relieved, because every payment was written down and nobody had to argue about who owed what. 🙂

qa.q: What alternative could work if someone forgets to log a payment on the road?
qa.a: They could pick one person to review the sheet each night, since small gaps are easier to fix on the same day.

qa.q: How might the two friends who quarrelled last year see this trip?
qa.a: They may see it as a calmer trip, because the sheet answered the money questions that caused trouble before.

grounding: A group opens a shared sheet, pays in advance and logs every expense, which avoids later disputes over money.

subtype: Approach: a shared expense sheet and advance deposit [Action]
passage:
Afreen, you're off to Coorg with seven friends? Before you go, let me, your Lalit uncle, tell you about my college trip to Ooty, and the fight that nearly ended a friendship.
We didn't keep track of anything. One person paid the bus, another the hotel, someone bought dinner, someone else the boat ride. On the last night we sat with a torn sheet of paper trying to remember who owed what. Voices rose. My friend Ravi said I was cheating him out of 300. I wasn't, but I couldn't prove it.
On the next trip we did it properly. Before leaving, each of us put 2,000 into one friend's account. Every payment came from there, and he wrote it in a notebook: date, what, how much. At the end, whatever was left was split back. No fights, no torn paper.
Now you have phones. Make a shared sheet. Put the money in one place first.

qa.q: How much did each friend put into one account on the next trip?
How did Lalit feel when Ravi said he was being cheated?
qa.a: Lalit felt hurt and helpless, knowing it wasn't true but unable to prove it.

qa.q: Which choice on the next trip prevented the arguments?
qa.a: Putting money into one account before leaving and writing down every payment, so the record settled things.

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt on that last night in Ooty?
qa.a: Ravi was probably frustrated and suspicious, unsure of the numbers, which made him lash out at a friend.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a messy trip without records, then a later trip with an upfront deposit in one account and every payment logged.

subtype: Approach: a shared expense sheet and advance deposit [Action]
passage:
In Tawang, the phone network came and went, which was a problem for a group of six whose money lived in a shared sheet. Farhan had set it up before the trip: each of them had put 3,000 into Pallavi's account, and every payment would be logged with date, item and amount.
On day two, the network vanished for eighteen hours. Pallavi paid the guesthouse in cash, then the taxi to the monastery, then a round of butter tea. Instead of trusting memory, Farhan wrote each one in the back of his diary, with the time.
When the signal returned in a café, he typed all nine entries into the sheet while the others ate. Spent so far: 11,400 of the 18,000.
On the last evening, one friend asked if the taxi had really cost 1,800. Pallavi just opened the sheet, and there it was, with the time next to it. The conversation moved on to photos.

qa.q: How much had each friend put into Pallavi's account?
Why did Farhan write the payments in his diary during the outage, and how might he have felt?
qa.a: He was probably a bit worried that things would be forgotten, and wanted to stay calm and fair by not trusting memory.

qa.q: What else could the group do if the network is patchy on the next trip?
qa.a: Choose one paper notebook as the backup from the start, so every payment has one place to go.

qa.q: How did the sheet help Pallavi on the last evening?
qa.a: Pallavi, who held the money, could answer a doubt at once without feeling accused, since the record showed the taxi and the time.

grounding: Shows a group with an upfront deposit in one account and a shared sheet, logging every payment even through a network outage, which heads off an argument.
